content: A blood transfusion is a critical medical intervention used to address life-threatening conditions in the short term. However, it is associated with potential adverse events, some of which may involve immune system modulation or the direct transmission of infectious agents, such as cytomegalovirus. Leukoreduction is a process designed to reduce the number of white blood cells in packed red blood cells (PRBCs) to minimize the risk of these adverse reactions. Despite its theoretical benefits, the effectiveness of leukoreduced PRBCs in reducing infectious and non-infectious complications across all patient populations remains uncertain. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness of leukoreduction in PRBCs for preventing adverse reactions following allogeneic blood transfusion. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and clinical trial registries was conducted, with the most recent search performed on November 10, 2015. Randomized clinical trials involving patients of all ages who required PRBC transfusion were included, regardless of the duration of follow-up or the country in which the study was conducted. The primary outcome assessed was transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), while secondary outcomes included death from any cause, infections, non-infectious complications, and other adverse events. Thirteen studies, primarily involving adult patients, met the inclusion criteria. The findings are as follows: 1. Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI): One trial involving 1864 trauma patients reported no significant difference between leukoreduced and non-leukoreduced PRBCs (Relative Risk [RR] 0.96, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.67 to 1.36, P = 0.80). The data represented only 28.5% of the required sample size for robust conclusions, and the quality of evidence was rated as low. 2. Death from Any Cause: Nine trials involving 6485 patients (including cardiovascular surgical, gastro-oncology surgical, trauma, and HIV-infected patients) showed no significant reduction in mortality with leukoreduction (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.12, I² = 63%, P = 0.20). The data represented 55.3% of the required sample size, and the quality of evidence was very low. 3. Infection from Any Cause: Ten trials involving 6709 patients (similar populations as above) found no significant reduction in infection rates with leukoreduction (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.03, I² = 84%, P = 0.08). The data represented 60.6% of the required sample size, and the quality of evidence was very low. 4. Adverse Events (Fever): Fever was the only adverse event specifically reported. Two trials involving 634 cardiovascular and gastro-oncology surgical patients showed no significant reduction in fever with leukoreduction (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.02, I² = 0%, P = 0.07). The data represented 84.4% of the required sample size, and the quality of evidence was low. 5. Non-Infectious Complications: No trials assessed the incidence of other non-infectious complications. In conclusion, there is no clear evidence to support or refute the routine use of leukoreduction in all patients requiring PRBC transfusion to prevent TRALI, death, infections, non-infectious complications, or other adverse events. The quality of evidence across all outcomes was rated as very low to low. Further high-quality research is necessary to draw definitive conclusions regarding the clinical benefits of leukoreduction.
